planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich soil in full to partial shade; this woodland species resents root disturbance once settled, so divide only when clumps become crowded.

directions: Set divisions into consistently moist, humus-rich woodland soil in full to partial shade in spring, mulching with leaf litter to mimic its native forest floor. Primula heucherifolia forms a low rosette of soft, rounded, velvety leaves resembling a heuchera, from which stand short stalks of umbels bearing magenta-pink flowers in mid spring. Native to the mountain forests of Sichuan and Yunnan, it pairs well with hepatica, trillium, and other spring woodland ephemerals and tends to thin or disappear in prolonged summer heat and drought. Keep soil evenly moist through the growing season and avoid letting it dry out during dormancy.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring into moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in dappled to full shade; give this close relative of Primula heucherifolia the same cool, consistently damp woodland conditions.

directions: Plant divisions in spring in evenly moist, humus-rich soil beneath deciduous shade, where the fine network of veins on its rounded, hairy leaves is most visible as new growth unfurls. Primula polyneura, native to the mountains of Gansu, Shaanxi, and Sichuan in China, sends up slender stalks carrying rose-purple flowers with a yellow throat in mid spring, just above the foliage mound. It closely resembles P. heucherifolia but has more deeply veined, sharply toothed leaves, and both make excellent companions for ferns and small hostas in a cool, shaded border. Provide steady moisture and protection from hot afternoon sun to keep foliage from scorching in summer.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Siberian primrose is one of the hardiest woodland primroses and tolerates cold winters without extra protection.

directions: Plant divisions in spring in humus-rich, moisture-retentive soil in dappled or partial shade; Siberian primrose is native across a wide swath of Siberia, the Russian Far East, Mongolia, and northern Japan and is correspondingly one of the toughest, most cold-hardy woodland primroses available to gardeners. Its softly hairy, scalloped leaves give rise to loose clusters of rose-pink flowers with a pale eye in mid to late spring, on short stems just above the foliage. It spreads gradually by short rhizomes to form a modest clump and combines well with corydalis, epimedium, and other small shade perennials in a woodland or rock garden setting. Give it protection from hot afternoon sun and consistent moisture through spring and early summer.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in consistently moist to wet, humus-rich soil at a stream or pond margin in partial shade in spring; this candelabra primrose needs reliably damp soil through summer.

directions: Set divisions into permanently moist to wet, humus-rich soil at a bog garden, stream, or pond margin in partial shade in spring. Primula aurantiaca, native to the mountains of Yunnan, China, produces a stout flower stalk bearing one or more whorls of small, deep orange to burnt-orange flowers in the classic candelabra arrangement in early summer, slightly earlier than many of its relatives. Its warm color is a useful foil for the pinks, magentas, and lilacs of P. japonica and P. bulleyana when planted together in a damp, partly shaded water garden. Like other candelabra primroses it declines quickly if the soil dries out, so site it only where moisture is dependable through the growing season.

planting.note: Plant divisions in consistently moist to wet, humus-rich soil at a bog or pond margin in partial shade in spring; give it the same damp, sheltered conditions favored by P. japonica and P. bulleyana.

directions: Plant divisions into reliably moist to wet, humus-rich soil at the edge of a bog garden, stream, or pond in partial shade in spring. Primula burmanica, native to the mountains of Yunnan and adjacent Myanmar, bears one or several stacked whorls of rich magenta-purple flowers with a small yellow eye on upright stems in early summer, in the same tiered candelabra form as P. japonica. It is one of the more vigorous candelabra species and will slowly naturalize into a colony along a permanently damp streambank where conditions suit it. Combine with astilbe, ligularia, and Japanese primrose for a layered display of color through a cool, moist, partly shaded planting.

planting.note: Plant divisions right after flowering in gritty, humus-rich, sharply drained soil in partial shade; this petiolarid primrose needs winter moisture but resents waterlogging, especially in summer.

directions: Divide and replant immediately after flowering into gritty, well-drained but humus-rich soil in a cool, partly shaded rock garden or raised bed, where a dusting of leaf litter can protect the crown over winter. Primula edgeworthii (long known in gardens as P. whitei) is a Himalayan rock garden primrose with small rosettes of farina-dusted, silvery-green leaves that produce clusters of lavender-blue to near-white flowers with a contrasting yellow eye in very early spring, often while snow still lingers nearby. Because its native habitat is rocky, humus-rich ledges with sharp drainage, it is less tolerant of soggy summer soil than most other shade primroses and is best suited to a scree bed or trough among other alpine treasures. Protect from hot sun and excess summer moisture to keep the compact rosettes healthy from year to year.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; this Himalayan woodlander wants steady moisture but not standing water.

directions: Plant divisions into moist, humus-rich, well-drained woodland soil in partial to full shade in spring, siting it where it will not bake in summer heat. Primula flaccida, native to the Himalaya and Yunnan, carries a loosely nodding cluster of soft lavender-blue, bell-shaped flowers dusted with pale farina atop slender stems in late spring, above a low rosette of long, textured leaves. The drooping, somewhat informal flower cluster gives it a quieter presence than the upright candelabra types, making it a good choice tucked among ferns and small woodland companions. Keep it consistently moist through summer and protect from drying wind, which quickly damages the mealy coating on its foliage and flowers.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; this East Asian woodland primrose is a close cousin of P. sieboldii and prefers similar cool, shaded conditions.

directions: Set divisions into moist, humus-rich soil in dappled to full shade in spring, ideally among rocks or fallen leaf litter that mimic its native forest-floor habitat. Primula saxatilis is native across the Russian Far East, Korea, Japan, and northeastern China, producing rounded, scalloped leaves and loose umbels of lilac-pink flowers with a pale center in mid spring, on short stems held just above the foliage. It is closely allied to P. sieboldii and P. cortusoides in appearance and culture, though it tends to hold its leaves a bit later into summer rather than disappearing completely. Grow it alongside hepatica, trillium, or small ferns in a shaded woodland garden with reliable spring and early-summer moisture.
